SQLite's own documentation says of the database file that "any process can open the file and overwrite it with garbage" (<https://www.sqlite.org/howtocorrupt.html>), and POSIX advisory locks "are useful only between cooperating processes" (<https://man7.org/linux/man-pages/man2/F_SETLK.2const.html>).
So the lock must not be recorded as the mechanism that closes this class. It closes the TOCTOU window against a
SQLite writer and makes the honest path atomic — which is real, and is what the controls exercise, since a store-writing attacker who uses SQLite is exactly what

models. What refuses a substituted lineage is the canonical digest, the unwritable root, and the compare-and-swap below. An attacker who bypasses SQLite's semantics entirely is out of scope, and would be caught at the next open rather than laundered into the root.

On the Memoir / Ariadne analogy, which does not carry here

R0.8.3 cites Memoir (Parno et al., IEEE S&P 2011) for safe replay and Ariadne (Strackx & Piessens, USENIX Security 2016) for the liveness requirement, and both citations stand. But neither is precedent for validate-at-open. In both systems, protected state lives in hardware-isolated memory once loaded and
the untrusted store is never read again during operation

; per-request validation is the default, not an addition. Memoir's own high-level specification states the invariant this round violated — that the service function's next input state is always its most recent output state — and its rollback-attack definition is a snapshot that is "internally consistent and cryptographically sound" yet ignores execution history, which is exactly a tampered-but-plausible store.

This controller re-reads a writable store on every mutation, so the structurally analogous requirement here is per-mutation validation. No paper found says "recovery-time validation is insufficient" in those words, because in that literature the question does not arise.
